section.paragraph: SO FAR WE HAVE DESCRIBED plane curves by giving $$y$$ as a function of $$x\left\lbrack {y = f(x)} \right\rbrack$$ or $$x$$ as a function of $$y\left\lbrack {x = g(y)} \right\rbrack$$ or by giving a relation between $$x$$ and $$y$$ that defines $$y$$ implicitly as a function of $$x\left\lbrack {f\left( {x,y} \right) = 0} \right\rbrack$$ . In this chapter we discuss two new methods for describing curves.

Some curves, such as the cycloid, are best handled when both $$x$$ and $$y$$ are given in terms of a third variable $$t$$ called a parameter $$\left\lbrack {x = f(t),y = g(t)} \right\rbrack$$ . Other curves, such as the cardioid, have their most convenient description when we use a new coordinate system, called the polar coordinate system.
section.heading: 10.1. Curves Defined by Parametric Equations
section.paragraph: Imagine that a particle moves along the curve $$C$$ shown in Figure 1. It is impossible to describe $$C$$ by an equation of the form $$y = f(x)$$ because $$C$$ fails the Vertical Line Test. But the $$x$$ - and $$y$$ -coordinates of the particle are functions of time and so we can write $$x = f(t)$$ and $$y = g(t)$$ . Such a pair of equations is often a convenient way of describing a curve.

section.heading: Parametric Equations
section.paragraph: Suppose that $$x$$ and $$y$$ are both given as functions of a third variable $$t$$ called a parameter, by the equations

which are called parametric equations. Each value of $$t$$ determines a point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ , which we can plot in a coordinate plane. As $$t$$ varies, the point $$\left( {x,y} \right) = \left( {f(t),g(t)} \right)$$ varies and traces out a curve called a parametric curve. The parameter $$t$$ does not necessarily represent time and, in fact, we could use a letter other than $$t$$ for the parameter. But in many applications of parametric curves, $$t$$ does denote time and in this case we can interpret $$\left( {x,y} \right) = \left( {f(t),g(t)} \right)$$ as the position of a moving object at time $$t$$ .

section.paragraph: It is not always possible to eliminate the parameter from parametric equations. There are many parametric curves that don’t have an equivalent representation as an equation in $$x$$ and $$y$$ .

In Example 1 we found a Cartesian equation in $$x$$ and $$y$$ whose graph coincided with the curve represented by parametric equations. This process is called eliminating the parameter; it can be helpful in identifying the shape of the parametric curve, but we lose some information in the process. The equation in $$x$$ and $$y$$ describes the curve the particle travels along, whereas the parametric equations have additional advantages—they tell us where the particle is at any given time and indicate the direction of motion. If you think of the graph of an equation in $$x$$ and $$y$$ as a road, then the parametric equations could track the motion of a car traveling along the road.

No restriction was placed on the parameter $$t$$ in Example 1, so we assumed that $$t$$ could be any real number (including negative numbers). But sometimes we restrict $$t$$ to lie in a particular interval. For instance, the parametric curve
$$x = t^{2} - 2t y = t + 1 0 \leqslant t \leqslant 4$$

section.paragraph: One of the most important uses of parametric curves is in computer-aided design (CAD). In the Discovery Project after Section 10.2 we will investigate special parametric curves, called Bézier curves, that are used extensively in manufacturing, especially in the automotive industry. These curves are also employed in specifying the shapes of letters and other symbols in PDF documents and laser printers.
section.heading: The Cycloid

example.heading: Example 9
example.paragraph: The curve traced out by a point $$P$$ on the circumference of a circle as the circle rolls along a straight line is called a cycloid. (Think of the path traced out by a pebble stuck in a car tire; see Figure 15.) If the circle has radius $$r$$ and rolls along the $$x$$ -axis and if one position of $$P$$ is the origin, find parametric equations for the cycloid.

image.alt: Details A series of arches standing on a horizontal line is displayed. A circle is drawn on the horizontal line such that the point it touches the line falls on the same point where the right leg of the second arch and the left leg of the third arch meets the line. This point is labeled P. example.paragraph: Solution We choose as parameter the angle of rotation $$\theta$$ of the circle ( $$\theta = 0$$ when $$P$$ is at the origin). Suppose the circle has rotated through $$\theta$$ radians. Because the circle has been in contact with the line, we see from Figure 16 that the distance it has rolled from the origin is
$$\left| {OT} \right| = {arc}PT = r\theta$$
Therefore the center of the circle is $$C\left( {r\theta,r} \right)$$ . Let the coordinates of $$P$$ be $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ . Then from Figure 16 we see that

$$\begin{array}{l} {x = \left| {OT} \right| - \left| {PQ} \right| = r\theta - r\sin\theta = r\left( {\theta - \sin\theta} \right)} \\ {y = \left| {TC} \right| - \left| {QC} \right| = r - r\cos\theta = r\left( {1 - \cos\theta} \right)} \end{array}$$
Therefore parametric equations of the cycloid are
$$x = r\left( {\theta - \sin\theta} \right) y = r\left( {1 - \cos\theta} \right) \theta \in {\mathbb{R}}$$

One arch of the cycloid comes from one rotation of the circle and so is described by $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ . Although Equations 1 were derived from Figure 16, which illustrates the case where $$0 < \theta < \pi \slash 2$$ , it can be seen that these equations are still valid for other values of $$\theta$$ (see Exercise 48).

section.paragraph: One of the first people to study the cycloid was Galileo; he proposed that bridges be built in the shape of cycloids and tried to find the area under one arch of a cycloid. Later this curve arose in connection with the brachistochrone problem: Find the curve along which a particle will slide in the shortest time (under the influence of gravity) from a point $$A$$ to a lower point $$B$$ not directly beneath $$A$$ . The Swiss mathematician John Bernoulli, who posed this problem in 1696, showed that among all possible curves that join $$A$$ to $$B$$ , as in Figure 17, the particle will take the least time sliding from $$A$$ to $$B$$ if the curve is part of an inverted arch of a cycloid.

section.paragraph: The Dutch physicist Huygens had already shown by 1673 that the cycloid is also the solution to the tautochrone problem; that is, no matter where a particle $$P$$ is placed on an inverted cycloid, it takes the same time to slide to the bottom (see Figure 18). Huygens proposed that pendulum clocks (which he invented) should swing in cycloidal arcs because then the pendulum would take the same time to make a complete oscillation whether it swings through a wide arc or a small arc.

example.paragraph: When $$a < - 1$$ , both branches are smooth; but when $$a$$ reaches $$- 1$$ , the right branch acquires a sharp point, called a cusp. For $$a$$ between $$- 1$$ and $$0$$ the cusp turns into a loop, which becomes larger as $$a$$ approaches $$0$$ . When $$a = 0$$ , both branches come together and form a circle (see Example 2). For $$a$$ between $$0$$ and $$1$$ , the left branch has a loop, which shrinks to become a cusp when $$a = 1$$ . For $$a > 1$$ , the branches become smooth again, and as $$a$$ increases further, they become less curved. Notice that the curves with $$a$$ positive are reflections about the $$y$$ -axis of the corresponding curves with $$a$$ negative.

These curves are called conchoids of Nicomedes after the ancient Greek scholar Nicomedes. He called them conchoids because the shape of their outer branches resembles that of a conch shell or mussel shell.

section.heading: 10.2. Calculus with Parametric Curves
section.paragraph: Having seen how to represent curves by parametric equations, we now apply the methods of calculus to these parametric curves. In particular, we solve problems involving tangents, areas, arc length, speed, and surface area.
section.heading: Tangents
section.paragraph: Suppose $$f$$ and $$g$$ are differentiable functions and we want to find the tangent line at a point on the parametric curve $$x = f(t)$$ , $$y = g(t)$$ , where $$y$$ is also a differentiable function of $$x$$ . Then the Chain Rule gives
$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} \cdot \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}$$
If $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} \neq 0$$ , we can solve for $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx}$$ :
$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}}}{\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}} \text{if} \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} \neq 0$$

If we think of the curve as being traced out by a moving particle, then $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt}$$ and $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt}$$ are the vertical and horizontal velocities of the particle and Formula 1 says that the slope of the tangent is the ratio of these velocities.

Equation 1 (which you can remember by thinking of canceling the $$\mathit{dt}$$ ’s) enables us to find the slope $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx}$$ of the tangent to a parametric curve without having to eliminate the parameter $$t$$ . We see from (1) that the curve has a horizontal tangent when $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt} = 0$$ , provided that $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} \neq 0$$ , and it has a vertical tangent when $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} = 0$$ , provided that $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt} \neq 0$$ . (If both $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} = 0$$ and $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt} = 0$$ , then we would need to use other methods to determine the slope of the tangent.) This information is useful for sketching parametric curves.
As we have learned, it is also often useful to consider $$d^{2}y/dx^{2}$$ . This can be found by replacing $$y$$ by $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx}$$ in Equation 1:
$$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = \frac{d}{dx}\left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} \right) = \frac{\frac{d}{dt}\left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} \right)}{\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}}$$
Note that $$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} \neq \frac{\frac{d^{2}y}{dt^{2}}}{\frac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}}}$$

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: A curve $$C$$ is defined by the parametric equations $$x = t^{2}$$ , $$y = t^{3} - 3t$$ .

list.item: (a) Show that $$C$$ has two tangents at the point $$(3,0)$$ and find their equations.
(b) Find the points on $$C$$ where the tangent is horizontal or vertical.
(c) Determine where the curve is concave upward or downward.
(d) Sketch the curve.

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) Notice that $$x = 3$$ for $$t = \pm \sqrt{3}$$ and, in both cases, $$y = t({t^{2} - 3}) = 0$$ . Therefore the point $$(3,0)$$ on $$C$$ arises from two values of the parameter, $$t = \sqrt{3}$$ and $$t = - \sqrt{3}$$ . This indicates that $$C$$ crosses itself at $$(3,0)$$ . Since $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt}}{\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt}} = \frac{3t^{2} - 3}{2t}$$ the slope of the tangent when $$t = \sqrt{3}$$ is $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx} = 6/(2\sqrt{3}) = \sqrt{3}$$ , and when $$t = - \sqrt{3}$$ the slope is $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx} = - 6/(2\sqrt{3}) = - \sqrt{3}$$ . Thus we have two different tangent lines at $$(3,0)$$ with equations $$y = \sqrt{3}{({x - 3})}$$ and $$y = - \sqrt{3}{({x - 3})}$$

(b) $$C$$ has a horizontal tangent when $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx} = 0$$ , that is, when $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt} = 0$$ and $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} \neq 0$$ . Since $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt} = 3t^{2} - 3$$ , this happens when $$t^{2} = 1$$ , that is, $$t = \pm 1$$ . The corresponding points on $$C$$ are $$(1, - 2)$$ and $$(1,2)$$ . $$C$$ has a vertical tangent when $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} = 2t = 0$$ , that is, $$t = 0$$ . (Note that $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt} \neq 0$$ there.) The corresponding point on $$C$$ is $$(0,0)$$ .

(c) To determine concavity we calculate the second derivative: $$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = \frac{\frac{d}{dt}\left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} \right)}{\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}} = \frac{\frac{d}{dt}\left( \frac{3t^{2} - 3}{2t} \right)}{\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}} = \frac{\frac{6t^{2} + 6}{4t^{2}}}{2t} = \frac{3t^{2} + 3}{4t^{3}}$$ Thus the curve is concave upward when $$t > 0$$ and concave downward when $$t < 0$$ .

(d) Using the information from parts (b) and (c), we sketch $$C$$ in Figure 1. Figure 1 Details A curve with a loop and four lines are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. Arrows are placed on the curve indicating the direction of the path it takes. The curve enters from the bottom right corner, goes up to the left, crosses the positive x-axis at (3, 0), goes up to the left, reaches a high point at (1, 2), descends downward, bulging to the left, touching the origin, reaches a low point at (1, negative 2), goes up to the right, crosses the x-axis again at (3, 0), and exits at the top right corner. The first line, labeled y = negative sqrt(3) (x minus 3) is tangent to the curve at (3, 0) as it climbs upward to the left. The second line labeled y = sqrt(3) (x minus 3) is tangent to the curve at (3, 0) as it climbs upward to the right. The third line, labeled t = 1 is tangent to the curve at its low point, (1, negative 2). The fourth line, labeled t = negative 1 is tangent to the curve at its high point, (1, 2).

example.heading: Example 2

list.item: (a) Find the tangent to the cycloid $$x = r(\theta - \sin\theta)$$ , $$y = r(1 - \cos\theta)$$ at the point where $$\theta = \pi/3$$ . (See Example 10.1.9.)
(b) At what points is the tangent horizontal? When is it vertical?

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) The slope of the tangent line is $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta} = \frac{r\sin\theta}{r(1 - \cos\theta)} = \frac{\sin\theta}{1 - \cos\theta}$$ When $$\theta = \pi/3$$ , we have $$x = r\left( {\frac{\pi}{3} - \sin\frac{\pi}{3}} \right) = r\left( {\frac{\pi}{3} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \right) y = r\left( {1 - \cos\frac{\pi}{3}} \right) = \frac{r}{2}$$ and $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{\sin\left( {\pi/3} \right)}{1 - \cos\left( {\pi/3} \right)} = \frac{\sqrt{3}/2}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{3}$$ Therefore the slope of the tangent is $$\sqrt{3}$$ and its equation is $$y - \frac{r}{2} = \sqrt{3}\left( {x - \frac{r\pi}{3} + \frac{r\sqrt{3}}{2}} \right)$$ or $$\sqrt{3}x - y = r\left( {\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}} - 2} \right)$$ The tangent is sketched in Figure 2. Figure 2 Details A cycloid and 10 lines tangent to it is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x-axis is displayed from negative 2 pi r to 6 pi r in increments of 2 pi r. Each arch of the cycloid has a width of 2 pi r. Five vertical lines are tangent to the cycloid at the points it touches the x-axis, namely, (negative 2 pi r, 0), (0, 0), (2 pi r, 0), (4 pi r, 0), and (6 pi r, 0). Four horizontal lines are tangent to the cycloid at the top most point of each arch, namely, (negative pi r, 2 r), (pi r, 2 r), (3 pi r, 2 r), and (5 pi r, 2 r). A line sloping upward to the right is tangent to the cycloid at a point labeled theta = pi/3, located on the cycloid as it rises upward to the right from the origin.

(b) The tangent is horizontal when $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx} = 0$$ , which occurs when $$\sin\theta = 0$$ and $$1 - \cos\theta \neq 0$$ , that is, $$\theta = (2n - 1)\pi$$ , $$n$$ an integer. The corresponding point on the cycloid is $$\left( (2n - 1)\pi r,2r \right)$$ . When $$\theta = 2n\pi$$ , both $$dx/d\theta$$ and $$dy/d\theta$$ are $$0$$ . It appears from the graph that there are vertical tangents at those points. We can verify this by using l’Hospital’s Rule as follows: $$\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow 2n\pi^{+}}\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow 2n\pi^{+}}\frac{\sin\theta}{1 - \cos\theta} = \lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow 2n\pi^{+}}\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \infty$$ A similar computation shows that $$\left. \mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx}\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ as $$\left. \theta\rightarrow 2n\pi^{-} \right.$$ , so indeed there are vertical tangents when $$\theta = 2n\pi$$ , that is, when $$x = 2n\pi r$$ . (See Figure 2.)

section.heading: Areas
section.paragraph: We know that the area under a curve $$y = F(x)$$ from $$a$$ to $$b$$ is $$A = {\int_{a}^{b}{F(x)dx}}$$ , where $$F(x) \geqslant 0$$ . If the curve is traced out once by the parametric equations $$x = f(t)$$ and $$y = g(t)$$ , $$\alpha \leqslant t \leqslant \beta$$ , then we can calculate an area formula by using the Substitution Rule for Definite Integrals as follows:
$$A = \int_{a}^{b}ydx = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta}g(t)f^{\prime}(t)dt \left\lbrack {or} \int_{\beta}^{\alpha}g(t)f^{\prime}(t)dt \right\rbrack$$
The limits of integration for $$t$$ are found as usual with the Substitution Rule. When $$x = a$$ , $$t$$ is either $$\alpha$$ or $$\beta$$ . When $$x = b$$ , $$t$$ is the remaining value.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find the area under one arch of the cycloid
$$x = r(\theta - \sin\theta) y = r(1 - \cos\theta)$$

image.alt: Details A cycloid is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x-axis is displayed from 0 to 2 pi r in increments of 2 pi r. The cycloid enters from the top left, goes down to the right, meets the x-axis at the origin, goes up to the right and then down to meet the x-axis at (2 pi r, 0), goes up to the right, and exits at the top right of the viewing window. The area under one full arch between x = 0 and x = 2 pi r is shaded.

example.paragraph: Solution One arch of the cycloid (shown in Figure 3) is given by $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ . Using the Substitution Rule with $$y = r(1 - \cos\theta)$$ and $$dx = r(1 - \cos\theta)d\theta$$ , we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = \int_{0}^{2\pi r}ydx = \int_{0}^{2\pi}r(1 - \cos\theta)r(1 - \cos\theta)d\theta} \\ {\phantom{A} = r^{2}\int_{0}^{2\pi}{(1 - \cos\theta)}^{2}d\theta = r^{2}\int_{0}^{2\pi}(1 - 2\cos\theta + \cos^{2}\theta)d\theta} \\ {\phantom{A} = r^{2}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left\lbrack {1 - 2\cos\theta + \frac{1}{2}(1 + \cos 2\theta)} \right\rbrack d\theta} \\ {\phantom{A} = r^{2}\left\lbrack \frac{3}{2}\theta - 2\sin\theta + \frac{1}{4}\sin 2\theta \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\pi}} \\ {\phantom{A} = r^{2}\left( \frac{3}{2} \cdot 2\pi \right) = 3\pi r^{2}} \end{array}$$

The result of Example 3 says that the area under one arch of the cycloid is three times the area of the rolling circle that generates the cycloid (see Example 10.1.9). Galileo guessed this result but it was first proved by the French mathematician Roberval and the Italian mathematician Torricelli.

section.heading: Arc Length
section.paragraph: We already know how to find the length $$L$$ of a curve $$C$$ given in the form $$y = F(x)$$ , $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ . Formula 8.1.3 says that if $$F^{\prime}$$ is continuous, then
$$L = {\int_{a}^{b}{\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} \right)^{2}}dx}}$$

Suppose that $$C$$ can also be described by the parametric equations $$x = f(t)$$ and $$y = g(t)$$ , $$\alpha \leqslant t \leqslant \beta$$ , where $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} = f^{\prime}(t) > 0$$ . This means that $$C$$ is traversed once, from left to right, as $$t$$ increases from $$\alpha$$ to $$\beta$$ and $$f(\alpha) = a$$ , $$f(\beta) = b$$ . Putting Formula 1 into Formula 2 and using the Substitution Rule, we obtain

$$L = {\int_{a}^{b}{\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} \right)^{2}}dx}} = {\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}{\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt}}{\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2}}\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}dt}}$$
Since $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} > 0$$ , we have
$$L = {\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\sqrt{\left( \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2}}dt}$$

Even if $$C$$ can’t be expressed in the form $$y = F(x)$$ , Formula 3 is still valid but we obtain it by polygonal approximations. We divide the parameter interval $$\left\lbrack {\alpha,\beta} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals of equal width $$\Delta t$$ . If $$t_{0},t_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{n}$$ are the endpoints of these subintervals, then $$x_{i} = f(t_{i})$$ and $$y_{i} = g(t_{i})$$ are the coordinates of points $$P_{i}(x_{i},y_{i})$$ that lie on $$C$$ and the polygonal path with vertices $$P_{0},P_{1},\ldots,P_{n}$$ approximates $$C$$ . (See Figure 4.)

image.alt: Details A curve, twelve points, and eleven line segments are graphed on the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The curve, labeled C, begins at a point labeled P_0, rises upward bulging to the left, passing through the points P_1 and P_2, runs horizontally to the right, bulging upward, passing through an unlabeled point, P_(i minus 1), and P_i, and then the curve descends downward bulging steeply slightly up and to the left, passing through five unlabeled points and ending at a point labeled P_n. Eleven line segments connect the first point on the curve to the second, the second point of the curve to the third, and so on.

section.paragraph: As in Section 8.1, we define the length $$L$$ of $$C$$ to be the limit of the lengths of these approximating polygonal paths as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ :
$$L = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\underset{i=1}{\overset{n}{\sum}}\left| {P_{i - 1}P_{i}} \right|$$
The Mean Value Theorem, when applied to $$f$$ on the interval $$\lbrack{t_{i - 1},t_{i}}\rbrack$$ , gives a number $$t_{i}^{*}$$ in $$({t_{i - 1},t_{i}})$$ such that
Let $$\Delta x_{i} = x_{i} - x_{i - 1}$$ and $$\Delta y_{i} = y_{i} - y_{i - 1}$$ . Then the preceding equation becomes
$$\Delta x_{i} = f^{\prime}(t_{i}^{*})\Delta t$$
Similarly, when applied to $$g$$ , the Mean Value Theorem gives a number $$t_{i}^{\ast \ast}$$ in $$({t_{i - 1},t_{i}})$$ such that
$$\Delta y_{i} = g^{\prime}(t_{i}^{\ast \ast})\Delta t$$
Therefore

$$\begin{matrix} {|{P_{i - 1}P_{i}}| = {\sqrt{{({\Delta x_{i}})}^{2} + {({\Delta y_{i}})}^{2}} = \sqrt{{\lbrack{{f^{\prime}}(t_{i}^{*})\Delta t}\rbrack}^{2} + {\lbrack{g^{\prime}(t_{i}^{**})\Delta t}\rbrack}^{2}}}} \\ {\phantom{|{P_{i - 1}P_{i}}|} = {\sqrt{{\lbrack{{f^{\prime}}(t_{i}^{*})}\rbrack}^{2} + {\lbrack{g^{\prime}(t_{i}^{**})}\rbrack}^{2}}\Delta t}} \end{matrix}$$
and so
$$L = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\underset{i=1}{\overset{n}{\sum}}{\sqrt{{\lbrack{{f^{\prime}}(t_{i}^{*})}\rbrack}^{2} + {\lbrack{g^{\prime}(t_{i}^{**})}\rbrack}^{2}}\Delta t}$$

The sum in (4) resembles a Riemann sum for the function $$\sqrt{{\lbrack{{f^{\prime}}(t)}\rbrack}^{2} + {\lbrack{g^{\prime}(t)}\rbrack}^{2}}$$ but it is not exactly a Riemann sum because $$t_{i}^{*} \neq t_{i}^{**}$$ in general. Nevertheless, if $$f^{\prime}$$ and $$g^{\prime}$$ are continuous, it can be shown that the limit in (4) is the same as if $$t_{i}^{*}$$ and $$t_{i}^{**}$$ were equal, namely,
$$L = {\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}{\sqrt{{\lbrack{{f^{\prime}}(t)}\rbrack}^{2} + {\lbrack{g^{\prime}(t)}\rbrack}^{2}}dt}}$$
Thus, using Leibniz notation, we have the following result, which has the same form as Formula 3.

note.title: Theorem
note.heading: Theorem
note.paragraph: If a curve $$C$$ is described by the parametric equations $$x = f(t)$$ , $$y = g(t)$$ , $$\alpha \leqslant t \leqslant \beta$$ , where $$f^{\prime}$$ and $$g^{\prime}$$ are continuous on $$\lbrack\alpha,\beta\rbrack$$ and $$C$$ is traversed exactly once as $$t$$ increases from $$\alpha$$ to $$\beta$$ , then the length of $$C$$ is

section.paragraph: Notice that the formula in Theorem 5 is consistent with the general formula $$L = {\int{ds}}$$ of Section 8.1, where
$$\mathit{ds} = \sqrt{\left( \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2}}\mathit{dt}$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: If we use the representation of the unit circle given in Example 10.1.2,
$$x = \cos t y = \sin t 0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2\pi$$
then $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} = - \sin t$$ and $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt} = \cos t$$ , so Theorem 5 gives

$$L = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sqrt{\left( \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2}}}dt = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{\sin^{2}t + \cos^{2}t}dt}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{dt}} = 2\pi$$
as expected. If, on the other hand, we use the representation given in Example 10.1.3,
$$x = \sin 2t y = \cos 2t 0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2\pi$$
then $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} = 2\cos 2t$$ , $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt} = - 2\sin 2t$$ , and the integral in Theorem 5 gives

$${\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sqrt{\left( \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2}}}dt = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sqrt{4\cos^{2}(2t) + 4\sin^{2}(2t)}}dt = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{2dt}} = 4\pi$$

Notice that the integral gives twice the arc length of the circle because as $$t$$ increases from $$0$$ to $$2\pi$$ , the point $$\left( \sin 2t,\cos 2t \right)$$ traverses the circle twice. In general, when finding the length of a curve $$C$$ from a parametric representation, we have to be careful to ensure that $$C$$ is traversed only once as $$t$$ increases from $$\alpha$$ to $$\beta$$ .

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Find the length of one arch of the cycloid $$x = r\left( \theta - \sin\theta \right)$$ , $$y = r(1 - \cos\theta)$$ .
Solution From Example 3 we see that one arch is described by the parameter interval $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ . Since
$$\frac{dx}{d\theta} = r(1 - \cos\theta)$$
and
$$\frac{dy}{d\theta} = r\sin\theta$$
we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {L = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{\left( \frac{dx}{d\theta} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{dy}{d\theta} \right)^{2}}d\theta}}} \\ {\phantom{L} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{r^{2}{({1 - \cos\theta})}^{2} + r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}d\theta}}} \\ {\phantom{L} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{r^{2}({1 - 2\cos\theta + \cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta})}d\theta}}} \\ {\phantom{L} = r{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{2({1 - \cos\theta})}d\theta}}} \end{array}$$

To evaluate this integral we use the identity $$\sin^{2}x = \frac{1}{2}{({1 - \cos 2x})}$$ with $$\theta = 2x$$ , which gives $$1 - \cos\theta = 2\sin^{2}(\theta/2)$$ . Since $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ , we have $$0 \leqslant \theta/2 \leqslant \pi$$ and so $$\sin(\theta/2) \geqslant 0$$ . Therefore
$$\sqrt{2(1 - \cos\theta)} = \sqrt{4\sin^{2}(\theta/2)} = 2\left| {\sin(\theta/2)} \right| = 2\sin(\theta/2)$$
and so
$$\begin{array}{l} {L = 2r{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sin(\theta/2)d\theta}} = 2r{\lbrack{- 2\cos(\theta/2)}\rbrack}_{0}^{2\pi}} \\ {\phantom{L} = 2r\lbrack 2 + 2\rbrack = 8r} \end{array}$$

The result of Example 5 says that the length of one arch of a cycloid is eight times the radius of the generating circle (see Figure 5). This was first proved in 1658 by Sir Christopher Wren, who later became the architect of St. Paul’s Cathedral in London.

section.paragraph: The arc length function and speed

Recall that the arc length function (Formula 8.1.5) gives the length of a curve from an initial point to any other point on the curve. For a parametric curve $$C$$ given by $$x = f(t)$$ , $$y = g(t)$$ , where $$f^{\prime}$$ and $$g^{\prime}$$ are continuous, we let $$s(t)$$ be the arc length along $$C$$ from an initial point $$(f(\alpha),g(\alpha))$$ to a point $$(f(t),g(t))$$ on $$C$$ . By Theorem 5, the arc length function $$s$$ for parametric curves is
$$s(t) = {\int_{\alpha}^{t}{\sqrt{\left( \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{du}} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{du}} \right)^{2}}du}}$$
(We have replaced the variable of integration by $$u$$ so that $$t$$ does not have two meanings.)

If parametric equations describe the position of a moving particle (with $$t$$ representing time), then the speed of the particle at time $$t$$ , $$v(t)$$ , is the rate of change of distance traveled (arc length) with respect to time: $$s^{\prime}(t)$$ . By Equation 7 and Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, we have
$$v(t) = s^{\prime}(t) = \sqrt{\left( \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2}}$$

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: The position of a particle at time $$t$$ is given by the parametric equations $$x = 2t + 3$$ , $$y = 4t^{2}$$ , $$t \geq 0$$ . Find the speed of the particle when it is at the point $$(5,4)$$ .
Solution By Equation 8, the speed of the particle at any time $$t$$ is

The particle is at the point $$(5,4)$$ when $$t = 1$$ , so its speed at that point is $$v(1) = 2\sqrt{17} \approx 8.25.$$ . (If distance is measured in meters and time in seconds, then the speed is approximately $$8.25m/s$$ .)

section.heading: Surface Area
section.paragraph: In the same way as for arc length, we can adapt Formula 8.2.5 to obtain a formula for surface area. Suppose a curve $$C$$ is given by the parametric equations $$x = f(t)$$ , $$y = g(t)$$ , $$\alpha \leqslant t \leqslant \beta$$ , where $$f^{\prime}$$ , $$g^{\prime}$$ are continuous, $$g(t) \geqslant 0$$ , and $$C$$ is traversed exactly once as $$t$$ increases from $$\alpha$$ to $$\beta$$ . If $$C$$ is rotated about the $$x$$ -axis, then the area of the resulting surface is given by
$$S = {\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}{2\pi y\sqrt{\left( \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2}}dt}}$$
The general symbolic formulas $$S = {\int{2\pi yds}}$$ and $$S = {\int{2\pi xds}}$$ (Formulas 8.2.7 and 8.2.8) are still valid, where $$\mathit{ds}$$ is given by Formula 6.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Show that the surface area of a sphere of radius $$r$$ is $$4\pi r^{2}$$ .
Solution The sphere is obtained by rotating the semicircle
$$x = r\cos t y = r\sin t 0 \leqslant t \leqslant \pi$$
about the $$x$$ -axis. Therefore, from Formula 9, we get

$$\begin{array}{l} {S = {\int_{0}^{\pi}{2\pi r\sin t\sqrt{{( - r\sin t)}^{2} + {({r\cos t})}^{2}}dt}}} \\ {\phantom{S} = 2\pi{\int_{0}^{\pi}{r\sin t\sqrt{r^{2}(\sin^{2}t + \cos^{2}t)}dt}} = 2\pi{\int_{0}^{\pi}{r\sin t \cdot rdt}}} \\ {\phantom{S} = 2\pi r^{2}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\sin tdt}} = 2\pi r^{2}( - \cos t)\rbrack_{0}^{\pi} = 4\pi r^{2}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: 10.3. Polar Coordinates
section.paragraph: A coordinate system represents a point in the plane by an ordered pair of numbers called coordinates. Usually we use Cartesian coordinates, which are directed distances from two perpendicular axes. Here we describe a coordinate system introduced by Newton, called the polar coordinate system, which is more convenient for many purposes.
section.heading: The Polar Coordinate System
section.paragraph: We choose a point in the plane that is called the pole (or origin) and is labeled $$O$$ . Then we draw a ray (half-line) starting at $$O$$ called the polar axis. This axis is usually drawn horizontally to the right and corresponds to the positive $$x$$ -axis in Cartesian coordinates.

If $$P$$ is any other point in the plane, let $$r$$ be the distance from $$O$$ to $$P$$ and let $$\theta$$ be the angle (usually measured in radians) between the polar axis and the line $$OP$$ as in Figure 1. Then the point $$P$$ is represented by the ordered pair $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ and $$r$$ , $$\theta$$ are called polar coordinates of $$P$$ . We use the convention that an angle is positive if measured in the counterclockwise direction from the polar axis and negative in the clockwise direction. If $$P = O$$ , then $$r = 0$$ and we agree that $$\left( {0,\theta} \right)$$ represents the pole for any value of $$\theta$$ .

section.heading: Relationship between Polar and Cartesian Coordinates
section.paragraph: The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates can be seen from Figure 5, in which the pole corresponds to the origin and the polar axis coincides with the positive $$x$$ -axis. If the point $$P$$ has Cartesian coordinates $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and polar coordinates $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ , then, from the figure, we have $$\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r}$$ and $$\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r}$$ . So to find the Cartesian coordinates $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ when the polar coordinates $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ are known, we use the equations
$$x = r\cos\theta y = r\sin\theta$$

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Convert the point $$\left( {2,\pi \slash 3} \right)$$ from polar to Cartesian coordinates.
Solution Since $$r = 2$$ and $$\theta = \pi \slash 3$$ , Equations 1 give
$$\begin{array}{l} {x = r\cos\theta = 2\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 1} \\ {y = r\sin\theta = 2\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = 2 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \sqrt{3}} \end{array}$$
Therefore the point is $$\left( {1,\sqrt{3}} \right)$$ in Cartesian coordinates.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Represent the point with Cartesian coordinates $$\left( {1, - 1} \right)$$ in terms of polar coordinates.
Solution If we choose $$r$$ to be positive, then Equations 2 give
$$\begin{array}{rcl} r & = & {\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} = \sqrt{1^{2} + \left( {- 1} \right)^{2}} = \sqrt{2}} \\ {\tan\theta} & = & {\frac{y}{x} = - 1} \end{array}$$

Since the point $$\left( {1, - 1} \right)$$ lies in the fourth quadrant, we can choose $$\theta = - \pi \slash 4$$ or $$\theta = 7\pi \slash 4$$ . Thus one possible answer is $$\left( {\sqrt{2}, - \pi \slash 4} \right)$$ ; another is $$\left( {\sqrt{2},7\pi \slash 4} \right)$$ .

section.paragraph: Note Equations 2 do not uniquely determine $$\theta$$ when $$x$$ and $$y$$ are given because, as $$\theta$$ increases through the interval $$0 \leqslant \theta < 2\pi$$ , each value of $$\tan\theta$$ occurs twice. Therefore, in converting from Cartesian to polar coordinates, it’s not good enough just to find $$r$$ and $$\theta$$ that satisfy Equations 2. As in Example 3, we must choose $$\theta$$ so that the point $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ lies in the correct quadrant.
section.heading: Polar Curves
section.paragraph: The graph of a polar equation $$r = f(\theta)$$ , or more generally $$F\left( {r,\theta} \right) = 0$$ , consists of all points $$P$$ that have at least one polar representation $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ whose coordinates satisfy the equation.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Sketch the curve $$r = 1 + \sin\theta$$ .

Solution Instead of plotting points as in Example 6, we first sketch the graph of $$r = 1 + \sin\theta$$ in Cartesian coordinates in Figure 10 by shifting the sine curve up one unit. This enables us to read at a glance the values of $$r$$ that correspond to increasing values of $$\theta$$ . For instance, we see that as $$\theta$$ increases from $$0$$ to $$\pi \slash 2$$ , $$r$$ (the distance from $$O$$ ) increases from $$1$$ to $$2$$ (see the corresponding green arrows in Figures 10 and 11), so we sketch the corresponding part of the polar curve in Figure 11(a). As $$\theta$$ increases from $$\pi \slash 2$$ to $$\pi$$ , Figure 10 shows that $$r$$ decreases from $$2$$ to $$1$$ , so we sketch the next part of the curve as in Figure 11(b). As $$\theta$$ increases from $$\pi$$ to $$3\pi \slash 2$$ , $$r$$ decreases from $$1$$ to $$0$$ as shown in part (c). Finally, as $$\theta$$ increases from $$3\pi \slash 2$$ to $$2\pi$$ , $$r$$ increases from $$0$$ to $$1$$ as shown in part (d). If we let $$\theta$$ increase beyond $$2\pi$$ or decrease beyond $$0$$ , we would simply retrace this path. Putting together the parts of the curve from Figure 11(a)–(d), we sketch the complete curve in part (e). It is called a cardioid because it’s shaped like a heart.

list.item: (a) If a polar equation is unchanged when $$\theta$$ is replaced by $$- \theta$$ , the curve is symmetric about the polar axis.

(b) If the equation is unchanged when $$r$$ is replaced by $$- r$$ , or when $$\theta$$ is replaced by $$\theta + \pi$$ , the curve is symmetric about the pole. (This means that the curve remains unchanged if we rotate it through $$180^{{^\circ}}$$ about the origin.)
(c) If the equation is unchanged when $$\theta$$ is replaced by $$\pi - \theta$$ , the curve is symmetric about the vertical line $$\theta = \pi \slash 2$$ .

section.paragraph: The curves sketched in Examples 6 and 8 are symmetric about the polar axis, since $$\cos\left( {- \theta} \right) = \cos\theta$$ . The curves in Examples 7 and 8 are symmetric about $$\theta = \pi \slash 2$$ because $$\sin\left( {\pi - \theta} \right) = \sin\theta$$ and $$\cos\left\lbrack 2{\left( {\pi - \theta} \right)\rbrack} = \cos 2\theta \right.$$ . The four-leaved rose is also symmetric about the pole. We could have used these symmetry properties in sketching the curves. For instance, in Example 6 we need only have plotted points for $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi \slash 2$$ and then reflected about the polar axis to obtain the complete circle.

example.heading: Example 9
example.paragraph: Graph the curve $$r = \sin\left( {8\theta \slash 5} \right)$$ .
Solution First we need to determine the domain for $$\theta$$ . So we ask ourselves: how many complete rotations are required until the curve starts to repeat itself? If the answer is $$n$$ , then
$$\sin\frac{8\left( {\theta + 2n\pi} \right)}{5} = \sin\left( {\frac{8\theta}{5} + \frac{16n\pi}{5}} \right) = \sin\frac{8\theta}{5}$$

and so we require that $$16n\pi \slash 5$$ be an even multiple of $$\pi$$ . This will first occur when $$n = 5$$ . Therefore we will graph the entire curve if we specify that $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 10\pi$$ . Figure 17 shows the resulting curve. Notice that this curve has $$16$$ loops.

example.heading: Example 10
example.paragraph: Investigate the family of polar curves given by $$r = 1 + c\sin\theta$$ . How does the shape change as $$c$$ changes? (These curves are called limaçons, after a French word for snail, because of the shape of the curves for certain values of $$c$$ .)

Solution Figure 18 shows computer-drawn graphs for various values of $$c$$ . (Note that we obtain the complete graph for $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ .) For $$c > 1$$ there is a loop that decreases in size as $$c$$ decreases. When $$c = 1$$ the loop disappears and the curve becomes the cardioid that we sketched in Example 7. For $$c$$ between $$1$$ and $$\frac{1}{2}$$ the cardioid’s cusp is smoothed out and becomes a “dimple.” When $$c$$ decreases from $$\frac{1}{2}$$ to $$0$$ , the limaçon is shaped like an oval. This oval becomes more circular as $$\left. c\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , and when $$c = 0$$ the curve is just the circle $$r = 1$$ .

section.heading: 10.4. Calculus in Polar Coordinates
section.paragraph: In this section we apply the methods of calculus to find areas, arc lengths, and tangents involving polar curves.
section.heading: Area
section.paragraph: To develop the formula for the area of a region whose boundary is given by a polar equation, we need to use the formula for the area of a sector of a circle:

where, as in Figure 1, $$r$$ is the radius and $$\theta$$ is the radian measure of the central angle. Formula 1 follows from the fact that the area of a sector is proportional to its central angle: $$A = (\theta \slash 2\pi)\pi r^{2} = \frac{1}{2}r^{2}\theta$$ . (See also Exercise 7.3.41.)

section.paragraph: Let $$\mathcal{R}$$ be the region, illustrated in Figure 2, bounded by the polar curve $$r = f(\theta)$$ and by the rays $$\theta = a$$ and $$\theta = b$$ , where $$f$$ is a positive continuous function and where $$0 < b - a \leqslant 2\pi$$ . We divide the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into subintervals with endpoints $$\theta_{0},\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\ldots,\theta_{n}$$ and equal width $$\Delta\theta$$ . The rays $$\theta = \theta_{i}$$ then divide $$\mathcal{R}$$ into $$n$$ smaller regions with central angle $$\Delta\theta = \theta_{i} - \theta_{i - 1}$$ . If we choose $$\theta_{i}^{\ast}$$ in the $$i$$ th subinterval $$\left\lbrack {\theta_{i - 1},\theta_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ , then the area $$\Delta A_{i}$$ of the $$i$$ th region is approximated by the area of the sector of a circle with central angle $$\Delta\theta$$ and radius $$f\left( \theta_{i}^{\ast} \right)$$ . (See Figure 3.)

section.paragraph: Thus from Formula 1 we have
$$\Delta A_{i} \approx \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {f\left( \theta_{i}^{\ast} \right)} \right\rbrack^{2}\Delta\theta$$
and so an approximation to the total area $$A$$ of $$\mathcal{R}$$ is
$$A \approx \underset{i=1}{\overset{n}{\sum}}{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack f\left( \theta_{i}^{*} \right) \right\rbrack^{2}\Delta\theta}$$

It appears from Figure 3 that the approximation in (2) improves as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ . But the sums in (2) are Riemann sums for the function $$g(\theta) = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {f(\theta)} \right\rbrack^{2}$$ , so

$$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\underset{i=1}{\overset{n}{\sum}}{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {f\left( \theta_{i}^{\ast} \right)} \right\rbrack^{2}\Delta\theta = {\int_{a}^{b}{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {f(\theta)} \right\rbrack^{2}d\theta}}}$$
It therefore appears plausible (and can in fact be proved) that the formula for the area $$A$$ of the polar region $$\mathcal{R}$$ is
$$A = {\int_{a}^{b}{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {f(\theta)} \right\rbrack^{2}d\theta}}$$

with the understanding that $$r = f(\theta)$$ . Note the similarity between Formulas 1 and 4.
When we apply Formula 3 or 4, it is helpful to think of the area as being swept out by a rotating ray through $$O$$ that starts with angle $$a$$ and ends with angle $$b$$ .

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Find the area of the region that lies inside the circle $$r = 3\sin\theta$$ and outside the cardioid $$r = 1 + \sin\theta$$ .

Solution The cardioid (see Example 10.3.7) and the circle are sketched in Figure 5 and the desired region is shaded. The values of $$a$$ and $$b$$ in Formula 3 are determined by finding the points of intersection of the two curves. They intersect when $$3\sin\theta = 1 + \sin\theta$$ . This gives $$\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2}$$ , so $$\theta = \pi \slash 6$$ , $$5\pi \slash 6$$ . The desired area can be found by subtracting the area inside the cardioid between $$\theta = \pi \slash 6$$ and $$\theta = 5\pi \slash 6$$ from the area inside the circle from $$\pi \slash 6$$ to $$5\pi \slash 6$$ . Thus
$$A = \frac{1}{2}{\int_{\pi \slash 6}^{5\pi \slash 6}{\left( {3\sin\theta} \right)^{2}d\theta - \frac{1}{2}{\int_{\pi \slash 6}^{5\pi \slash 6}{\left( {1 + \sin\theta} \right)^{2}d\theta}}}}$$
Since the region is symmetric about the vertical axis $$\theta = \pi \slash 2$$ , we can write

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {2\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{2}{\int_{\pi \slash 6}^{\pi \slash 2}{9\sin^{2}\theta d\theta - \frac{1}{2}{\int_{\pi \slash 6}^{\pi \slash 2}{{({1 + 2\sin\theta + \sin^{2}\theta})}d\theta}}}}} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\int_{\pi \slash 6}^{\pi \slash 2}{{({8{\sin}^{2}\theta - 1 - 2\sin\theta})}d\theta}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\int_{\pi \slash 6}^{\pi \slash 2}{\left( {3 - 4\cos 2\theta - 2\sin\theta} \right)d\theta}} \left\lbrack {because}\sin^{2}\theta = \frac{1}{2}\left( {1 - \cos 2\theta} \right) \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{A} = {3\theta - 2\sin 2\theta + 2\cos\theta}{\rbrack_{\pi \slash 6}^{\pi \slash 2}{= \pi}}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: Example 2 illustrates the procedure for finding the area of the region bounded by two polar curves. section.paragraph: Caution The fact that a single point has many representations in polar coordinates sometimes makes it difficult to find all the points of intersection of two polar curves. For instance, it is obvious from Figure 5 that the circle and the cardioid have three points of intersection; however, in Example 2 we solved the equations $$r = 3\sin\theta$$ and $$r = 1 + \sin\theta$$ and found only two such points, $$\left( {\frac{3}{2},\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ and $$\left( {\frac{3}{2},5\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ . The origin is also a point of intersection, but we can’t find it by solving the equations of the curves because the origin has no single representation in polar coordinates that satisfies both equations. Notice that, when represented as $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ or $$\left( {0,\pi} \right)$$ , the origin satisfies $$r = 3\sin\theta$$ and so it lies on the circle; when represented as $$\left( {0,3\pi \slash 2} \right)$$ , it satisfies $$r = 1 + \sin\theta$$ and so it lies on the cardioid. Think of two points moving along the curves as the parameter value $$\theta$$ increases from $$0$$ to $$2\pi$$ . On one curve the origin is reached at $$\theta = 0$$ and $$\theta = \pi$$ ; on the other curve it is reached at $$\theta = 3\pi \slash 2$$ . The points don’t collide at the origin because they reach the origin at different times, but the curves intersect there nonetheless. (See also Exercises 10.1.55, 10.1.56, and 10.1.57.)

Thus, to find all points of intersection of two polar curves, it is recommended that you draw the graphs of both curves. It is especially convenient to use a graphing calculator or computer to help with this task.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find all points of intersection of the curves $$r = \cos 2\theta$$ and $$r = \frac{1}{2}$$ .

Solution If we solve the equations $$r = \cos 2\theta$$ and $$r = \frac{1}{2}$$ simultaneously, we get $$\cos 2\theta = \frac{1}{2}$$ and, therefore, $$2\theta = \pi \slash 3$$ , $$5\pi \slash 3$$ , $$7\pi \slash 3$$ , $$11\pi \slash 3$$ . Thus the values of $$\theta$$ between $$0$$ and $$2\pi$$ that satisfy both equations are $$\theta = \pi \slash 6$$ , $$5\pi \slash 6$$ , $$7\pi \slash 6$$ , $$11\pi \slash 6$$ . We have found four points of intersection: $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ , $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},5\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ , $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},7\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},11\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ .

However, you can see from Figure 7 that the curves have four other points of intersection—namely, $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},\pi \slash 3} \right)$$ , $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},2\pi \slash 3} \right)$$ , $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},4\pi \slash 3} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},5\pi \slash 3} \right)$$ . These can be found using symmetry or by noticing that another equation of the circle is $$r = - \frac{1}{2}$$ and then solving the equations $$r = \cos 2\theta$$ and $$r = - \frac{1}{2}$$ simultaneously.

section.heading: Arc Length
section.paragraph: Recall from Section 10.3 that rectangular coordinates $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and polar coordinates $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ are related by the equations $$x = r\cos\theta$$ , $$x = r\sin\theta$$ . Regarding $$\theta$$ as a parameter allows us to write parametric equations for a polar curve $$r = f(\theta)$$ as follows.
$$x = r\cos\theta = f(\theta)\cos\theta y = r\sin\theta = f(\theta)\sin\theta$$
Parametric equations for a polar curve
To find the length of a polar curve $$r = f(\theta)$$ , $$a \leqslant \theta \leqslant b$$ , we start with Equations 5 and differentiate with respect to $$\theta$$ (using the Product Rule):
$$\frac{dx}{d\theta} = \frac{dr}{d\theta}\cos\theta - r\sin\theta \frac{dy}{d\theta} = \frac{dr}{d\theta}\sin\theta + r\cos\theta$$
Then, using $$\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta = 1$$ , we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\left( \frac{dx}{d\theta} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{dy}{d\theta} \right)^{2} = \left( \frac{dr}{d\theta} \right)^{2}\cos^{2}\theta - 2r\frac{dr}{d\theta}\cos\theta\sin\theta + r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta} \\ {{+ \left( \frac{dr}{d\theta} \right)^{2}\sin^{2}\theta + 2r\frac{dr}{d\theta}\sin\theta\cos\theta + r^{2}{\cos}^{2}\theta}} \\ {\phantom{\left( \frac{dx}{d\theta} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{dy}{d\theta} \right)^{2}} = {\left( \frac{dr}{d\theta} \right)^{2} + r^{2}}} \end{array}$$
Assuming that $$f^{\prime}$$ is continuous, we can use Theorem 10.2.5 to write the arc length as
$$L = {\int_{a}^{b}{\sqrt{\left( \frac{dx}{d\theta} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{dy}{d\theta} \right)^{2}}d\theta}}$$
Therefore the length of a curve with polar equation $${r = f(\theta)},{a \leqslant \theta \leqslant b}$$ , is
$$L = {\int_{a}^{b}{\sqrt{r^{2} + \left( \frac{dr}{d\theta} \right)^{2}}d\theta}}$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find the length of the cardioid $$r = 1 + \sin\theta$$ .
Solution The cardioid is shown in Figure 8. (We sketched it in Example 10.3.7.) Its full length is given by the parameter interval $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ , so Formula 6 gives

$$L = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{r^{2} + \left( \frac{dr}{d\theta} \right)^{2}}d\theta = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{\left( {1 + \sin\theta} \right)^{2} + \cos^{2}\theta^{}}d\theta = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{2 + 2\sin\theta^{}}d\theta}}}}}}$$

We could evaluate this integral by multiplying and dividing the integrand by $$\sqrt{2 - 2\sin\theta}$$ , or we could use mathematical software. In any event, we find that the length of the cardioid is $$L = 8$$ .

section.heading: Tangents
section.paragraph: To find a tangent line to a polar curve $$r = f(\theta)$$ , we again regard $$\theta$$ as a parameter and write parametric equations for the curve following Equations 5:
$$x = r\cos\theta = f(\theta)\cos\theta y = r\sin\theta = f(\theta)\sin\theta$$
Then, using the method for finding the slope of a parametric curve (Equation 10.2.1) and the Product Rule, we have
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{dy}{d\theta}}{\frac{dx}{d\theta}} = \frac{\frac{dr}{d\theta}\sin\theta + r\cos\theta}{\frac{dr}{d\theta}\cos\theta - r\sin\theta}$$

We locate horizontal tangents by finding the points where $$dy \slash d\theta = 0$$ (provided that $$dx \slash d\theta \neq 0$$ ). Likewise, we locate vertical tangents at the points where $$dx \slash d\theta = 0$$ (provided that $$dy \slash d\theta \neq 0$$ ).
Notice that if we are looking for tangent lines at the pole, then $$r = 0$$ and Equation 7 simplifies to
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \tan\theta {if}\frac{dr}{d\theta} \neq 0$$

For instance, in Example 10.3.8 we found that $$r = \cos 2\theta = 0$$ when $$\theta = \pi \slash 4$$ or $$3\pi \slash 4$$ . This means that the lines $$\theta = \pi \slash 4$$ and $$\theta = 3\pi \slash 4$$ (or $$y = x$$ and $$y = - x$$ ) are tangent lines to $$r = \cos 2\theta$$ at the origin.

example.heading: Example 5

list.item: (a) For the cardioid $$r = 1 + \sin\theta$$ of Example 4, find the slope of the tangent line when $$\theta = \pi \slash 3$$ .
(b) Find the points on the cardioid where the tangent line is horizontal or vertical.

example.paragraph: Solution Using Equation 7 with $$r = 1 + \sin\theta$$ , we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{dr}{d\theta}\sin\theta + r\cos\theta}{\frac{dr}{d\theta}\cos\theta - r\sin\theta} = \frac{\cos\theta\sin\theta + \left( 1 + \sin\theta \right)\cos\theta}{\cos\theta\cos\theta - \left( 1 + \sin\theta \right)\sin\theta}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{dy}{dx}} = \frac{\cos\theta\left( {1 + 2\sin\theta} \right)}{1 - 2{\sin}^{2}\theta - \sin\theta} = \frac{\cos\theta\left( {1 + 2\sin\theta} \right)}{\left( {1 + \sin\theta} \right)\left( {1 - 2\sin\theta} \right)}} \end{array}$$

list.item: (a) The slope of the tangent at the point where $$\theta = \pi \slash 3$$ is $$\begin{array}{l} {\left. \frac{dy}{dx} \right|_{\theta = \pi \slash 3} = \frac{\cos\left( {\pi \slash 3} \right)\left\lbrack {1 + 2\sin\left( {\pi \slash 3} \right)} \right\rbrack}{\left\lbrack {1 + \sin\left( {\pi \slash 3} \right)} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack {1 - 2\sin\left( {\pi \slash 3} \right)} \right\rbrack} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\left( {1 + \sqrt{3}} \right)}{\left( {1 + \sqrt{3} \slash 2} \right)\left( {1 - \sqrt{3}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\left. \frac{dy}{dx} \right|_{\theta = \pi \slash 3}} = \frac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{\left( {2 + \sqrt{3}} \right)\left( {1 - \sqrt{3}} \right)} = {\frac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{- 1 - \sqrt{3}} = - 1}} \end{array}$$

(b) Observe that $$\begin{array}{ll} {\frac{dy}{d\theta} = \cos\theta\left( {1 + 2\sin\theta} \right) = 0} & {{when}\theta = \frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2},\frac{7\pi}{6},\frac{11\pi}{6}} \\ {\frac{dx}{d\theta} = \left( {1 + \sin\theta} \right)\left( {1 - 2\sin\theta} \right) = 0} & {{when}\theta = \frac{3\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{5\pi}{6}} \end{array}$$

example.paragraph: Therefore there are horizontal tangents at the points $$\left( {2,\pi \slash 2} \right)$$ , $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},7\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ , $$\left( {\frac{1}{2},11\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ and vertical tangents at $$\left( {\frac{3}{2},\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ and $$\left( {\frac{3}{2},5\pi \slash 6} \right)$$ . When $$\theta = 3\pi \slash 2$$ , both $$dy \slash d\theta$$ and $$dx \slash d\theta$$ are $$0$$ , so we must be careful. Using l’Hospital’s Rule, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow{({3\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}\frac{dy}{dx} = \left( {\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow{({3\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}\frac{1 + 2\sin\theta}{1 - 2\sin\theta}} \right)\left( {\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow{({3\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}\frac{\cos\theta}{1 + \sin\theta}} \right)} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow{({3\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}\frac{dy}{dx}}{= - \frac{1}{3}\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow{({3\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}\frac{\cos\theta}{1 + \sin\theta} = - \frac{1}{3}\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow{({3\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}\frac{- \sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \infty}} \end{array}$$
By symmetry,
$$\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow{({3\pi \slash 2})}^{+}}\frac{dy}{dx} = - \infty$$

section.paragraph: In this section we give geometric definitions of parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas and derive their standard equations. They are called conic sections, or conics, because they result from intersecting a cone with a plane as shown in Figure 1.

section.heading: Parabolas
section.paragraph: A parabola is the set of points in a plane that are equidistant from a fixed point $$F$$ (called the focus) and a fixed line (called the directrix). This definition is illustrated by Figure 2. Notice that the point halfway between the focus and the directrix lies on the parabola; it is called the vertex. The line through the focus perpendicular to the directrix is called the axis of the parabola.

section.paragraph: In the 16th century Galileo showed that the path of a projectile that is shot into the air at an angle to the ground is a parabola. Since then, parabolic shapes have been used in designing automobile headlights, reflecting telescopes, and suspension bridges. (See Problem 22 in Problems Plus following Chapter 3 for the reflection property of parabolas that makes them so useful.)

We obtain a particularly simple equation for a parabola if we place its vertex at the origin $$O$$ and its directrix parallel to the $$x$$ -axis as in Figure 3. If the focus is the point $$(0,p)$$ , then the directrix has the equation $$y = - p$$ . If $$P(x,y)$$ is any point on the parabola, then the distance from $$P$$ to the focus is
$$\left| {PF} \right| = \sqrt{x^{2} + (y - p)^{2}}$$
and the distance from $$P$$ to the directrix is $$|y + p|$$ . (Figure 3 illustrates the case where $$p > 0$$ .) The defining property of a parabola is that these distances are equal:
$$\sqrt{x^{2} + (y - p)^{2}} = \left| {y + p} \right|$$

section.paragraph: Like parabolas, ellipses have an interesting reflection property that has practical consequences. If a source of light or sound is placed at one focus of a surface with elliptical cross-sections, then all the light or sound is reflected off the surface to the other focus (see Exercise 67). This principle is used in lithotripsy, a treatment for kidney stones. A reflector with elliptical cross-section is placed in such a way that the kidney stone is at one focus. High-intensity sound waves generated at the other focus are reflected to the stone and destroy it without damaging surrounding tissue. The patient is spared the trauma of surgery and recovers within a few days.

section.heading: Kepler’s Laws
section.paragraph: In 1609 the German mathematician and astronomer Johannes Kepler, on the basis of huge amounts of astronomical data, published the following three laws of planetary motion.

list.item: A planet revolves around the sun in an elliptical orbit with the sun at one focus.
The line joining the sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times.
The square of the period of revolution of a planet is proportional to the cube of the length of the major axis of its orbit.

section.paragraph: Although Kepler formulated his laws in terms of the motion of planets around the sun, they apply equally well to the motion of moons, comets, satellites, and other bodies that orbit subject to a single gravitational force. In Section 13.4 we will show how to deduce Kepler’s Laws from Newton’s Laws. Here we use Kepler’s First Law, together with the polar equation of an ellipse, to calculate quantities of interest in astronomy.

For purposes of astronomical calculations, it’s useful to express the equation of an ellipse in terms of its eccentricity $$e$$ and its semimajor axis $$a$$ . We can write the distance $$d$$ from the focus to the directrix in terms of $$a$$ if we use (4):
So $$ed = a(1 - e^{2})$$ . If the directrix is $$x = d$$ , then the polar equation is
$$r = \frac{ed}{1 + e\cos\theta} = \frac{a(1 - e^{2})}{1 + e\cos\theta}$$
The polar equation of an ellipse with focus at the origin, semimajor axis $$a$$ , eccentricity $$e$$ , and directrix $$x = d$$ can be written in the form
$$r = \frac{a(1 - e^{2})}{1 + e\cos\theta}$$

The positions of a planet that are closest to and farthest from the sun are called its perihelion and aphelion, respectively, and correspond to the vertices of the ellipse (see Figure 7). The distances from the sun to the perihelion and aphelion are called the perihelion distance and aphelion distance, respectively. In Figure 1 the sun is at the focus $$F$$ , so at perihelion we have $$\theta = 0$$ and, from Equation 7,
$$r = \frac{a\left( 1 - e^{2} \right)}{1 + e\cos 0} = \frac{a(1 - e)(1 + e)}{1 + e} = a(1 - e)$$
Similarly, at aphelion $$\theta = \pi$$ and $$r = a(1 + e)$$ .

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) The length of the major axis is $$2a = 2.99 \times 10^{8}$$ , so $$a = 1.495 \times 10^{8}$$ . We are given that $$e = 0.017$$ and so, from Equation 7, an equation of the earth’s orbit around the sun is $$r = \frac{a(1 - e^{2})}{1 + e\cos\theta} = \frac{(1.495 \times 10^{8})\lbrack 1 - \left. (0.017 \right)^{2}\rbrack}{1 + 0.017\cos\theta}$$ or, approximately, $$r = \frac{1.49 \times 10^{8}}{1 + 0.017\cos\theta}$$
